conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you’ve been having a tough time with nausea and pain since your procedure earlier today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, right after they fixed my femoral line, I started feeling that familiar migraine and then couldn’t stop vomiting—green, bilious stuff. I haven’t been able to keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your abdominal pain—is it in the same areas as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly the same—left upper quadrant and around my belly button. It’s constant, and I’d say it’s about a 10. It feels just like my past obstruction episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve reviewed your imaging from today—a KUB shows air-fluid levels and dilated bowel, consistent with a partial small bowel obstruction. No free air, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not worse than last time? But why can’t I keep anything down now when I could before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your gut motility has been chronically impaired, and with the adhesions from your past surgeries, even small changes can trigger this. We’re going to keep your G-tube on suction to help decompress your bowel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain? It’s unbearable. I’ve been on Dilaudid in the ED, but even that barely touches it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you IV Dilaudid in small doses every few hours, just like your ED protocol. We also consulted pain management, but they agree it’s very difficult to control with your allergy history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just wish there was something more definitive. I’ve heard about PCA pumps—could that work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pain service suggested rectal Dilaudid as an outpatient option since PCA isn’t feasible without a willing primary doctor. We’re going to try a 3 mg suppository as needed every 3 hours when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds better than nothing. But surgery—has anyone talked to Dr. ___? I feel like it’s the only real solution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted general surgery, including your prior surgeon. They feel given your extensive adhesions, another surgery would be too risky and unlikely to help. The risk of volvulus is low because your bowel is so scarred down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s risky… but living like this isn’t living. I’ve been feeling so hopeless lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’ve noted your depressive symptoms and will make sure your psychiatrist is looped in. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning are stable—your hemoglobin is a bit low at 9.8, but that’s your baseline. No signs of infection or organ failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the liver enzymes? I’ve had Hep C for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Slightly elevated AST and alkaline phosphatase, but nothing acute. We’ll keep monitoring, but it’s likely chronic changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My G-tube is draining a lot—green, fecal-like fluid. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s expected. It means we’re decompressing your bowel effectively. You’re draining several hundred cc’s a day, which supports the obstruction picture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been talking with your outpatient team—your GI, pain specialist, and primary doctor. They agree your pain is extremely hard to manage, but options are limited.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And? Did they have any new ideas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not really. They support continuing your current meds and adding the rectal Dilaudid at home. We also discussed long-term care or hospice, but I understand you’re not ready for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’m only 50. I want to keep fighting. I know it’s bad, but I’m not giving up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we respect that. You’re a full code, and we’ll continue supporting you at home with TPN, fluids, and symptom control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your nausea has improved a bit. We’ve switched from IV Phenergan to liquid form for when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I hate shots. Can I start drinking anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Your bowel is still sluggish. We’ll keep you on TPN and IV fluids for now. We’re cycling 2.5 liters of saline daily at 150 cc per hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your G-tube output has decreased slightly—from 800 cc to about 500 cc per day. That’s a small sign of improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s something. My pain is still terrible, though. The IV Dilaudid helps a little, but it fades fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving it every 6 hours in a slow infusion. It’s the safest way to manage it here. At home, the suppository should offer more flexibility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in a few days. Your labs are stable, and your vitals are normal. You’re still not tolerating food, but that’s expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared to go home. What if I get worse and can’t reach anyone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your weekly ED visits for Dilaudid. And if you vomit more or your pain spikes, come back right away. Your femoral line is stable, so we can give fluids quickly if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve finalized your discharge meds. We’re simplifying a few things—lowering your trazodone and amitriptyline doses to reduce sedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so tired. Maybe that’ll help. What about my Abilify? Last time they lowered it for dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on 2 mg now, which is your stable dose. We’re keeping it the same. Your dizziness isn’t an issue this admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your hemoglobin dipped to 9.3, but it’s not falling. Your electrolytes are normal, and kidney function is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Anemia again. Is it from bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of acute bleeding. It’s likely chronic, from your GI losses and nutritional challenges. We’re continuing your iron and multivitamins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling your discharge for tomorrow. You’ll go home with services to help with your TPN and G-tube care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous, but I guess I have to. Will my pain ever get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t promise that. But we can keep adjusting your comfort. The rectal Dilaudid may give you more control. And we’ll keep talking with your team about new options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day. Your exam shows you’re alert, pain is stable, and your G-tube is draining green material but no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? I’ve been feeling it race.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart rate is in the 80s now—much better than the 120s you usually run. Your EKG was normal, no ischemia. Your mitral valve issue remains stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I don’t need another thing to worry about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending you home with TPN set to cycle over 12 hours each day—2200 ml with all your nutrients. And 2.5 liters of saline daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same as before. I can manage that. And the new suppository—I’ll use it only when the pain is unbearable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. One 3 mg suppository every 3 hours as needed. And liquid Phenergan for nausea. Call your doctor if you’re using them more than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll keep seeing my psychiatrist. I’ve been having dark thoughts, but no plans.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for sharing that. Please keep talking to her. You’re not alone, and we care about your mental health too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. It means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have weekly labs—CBC, chem-10, albumin. Fax them to your GI doctor. And follow up with Dr. ___ in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll make sure it’s done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also keep your femoral line monitored. No redness or issues now, but let us know if it becomes tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you, Dr. Lee. I know I’m a tough case, but you’ve been kind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re strong, and we’re here to support you. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick call to check in. How are you holding up at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous, but the suppository helps the pain a bit. G-tube draining about 400 cc. I used Phenergan twice yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s within expected range. Keep up with fluids and TPN. If output increases or you feel worse, come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for checking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re officially closing your admission. You were in for about 12 days, and we’re discharging you from our records now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll keep following the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot. Take it one day at a time. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Talk soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we can ask.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well.
